newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee ends lackluster session mixed.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee ends lackluster session mixed.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures ended mixed in sluggish trading on Friday, as the market's attempt to rebound from Thursday's sharp sell-off ran into a late-session bout of local selling, dealers said.

Benchmark September arabicas rose 3.20 cents per lb on the day, to 169.30, after ranging from 173.00 to 166.25. Spot July finished 0.35 cent weaker, at 189.90, while the outer months closed up 2.90 to down 2.85.
Volume was light, at an estimated 5,129 lots.
The July/September switch shrank to 20.60 cents, from 24.15 cents at the close on Thursday, while September/December widened to 20.30 cents compared with 19.85 cents.

Technically, traders pegged September resistance at the 174.00-175.00 level, with the next upside hurdle at Thursday's high of 181.00. Strong support was seen at 165.00 cents, yesterday's low, they said.
Some traders said continued mild weather in top-grower Brazil and talk of a build up in stocks pending CSCE certification would weigh on the market.
But some Brazilian meterologists said the recent wave of warm weather in the country's coffee-growing regions may be due to the El Nino, which they said could have some unwelcome, rainy implications.

Brazil's coffee regions saw unseasonal rains this month which have delayed the harvest and impacted the quality of the beans, growers said. They also noted the occurence of early scattered flowerings -- the first stage in the development of next's year's harvest -- which normally begin at the end of August, beginning of September.
However, growers also noted that the rains brought favorable moisture to the soil which could help the development of the 1998/99 crop.
After Friday's close, CSCE reported certified coffee stocks fell by 280 60-kg bags as of June 26, to 45,893 bags. However, there were 14,594 bags pending grading, the exchange said.

Also after the close on Friday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture released coffee production, supply and distribution balances -- based on the production data released June 13 -- in its bulletin Tropical Products: World Markets & Trade.
The USDA data showed 1997/98 beginning stocks of coffee in producing countries at 26 million 60-kg bags, their lowest level since 1980/81.
"It shows supplies are still tight," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "If there's any kind of weather problems at some point the well runs dry.
"The export figure, I'm not sure how producers will manage it," she added. "It seems ambitious."

USDA estimated 1997/98 world coffee exports at 84.4 million 60-kilogram bags, up from a revised 82.9 million bags seen in 1996/97. USDA previously pegged 1996/97 world coffee exports at 79.6 million bags.

USDA said total coffee supply in producing countries in 1997/98 is forecast at 130.5 million bags, down 2.5 percent from the prior year largely due to the lower beginning stock levels. It forecast 1997/98 ending stocks in producing countries at 20 million bags.
Earlier this month, USDA forecast 1997/98 world coffee production at 103.7 million bags and estimated the Brazil crop at 28.0 million bags.
